fixes.explanation: A pillar of fire does show up in the Bible, but later, when the LORD goes ahead of Israel by night (Exodus 13:21). Here in Genesis 8:1, God sends a wind over the earth. Fire belongs to a whole different batch of dough, friend.

Not in a single day, friend. The text says "The waters receded steadily from the earth, and after 150 days the waters had gone down." (Genesis 8:3) Steadily, not suddenly. It's like a bathtub with a slow drain, and nobody gets to hurry it.

Ararat it is. "On the seventeenth day of the seventh month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat." (Genesis 8:4) After all that floating, the ark finally has something solid under it. I bet everybody on board felt that bump.

Samaria comes much later in the Bible. Omri, a king of Israel, bought the hill of Samaria and built a city there (1 Kings 16:24). That's not where the ark lands. Genesis 8:4 says it came to rest on the mountains of Ararat.

Mountains! "…on the first day of the tenth month the tops of the mountains became visible." (Genesis 8:5) The waters had been receding up to that point, and now the tops of the mountains show. I bet Noah looked at that view for a good long while.

No towers in this verse, friend. In Genesis 8:5, what becomes visible is the tops of the mountains. A tower does get built later in Genesis, at Babel (Genesis 11:4). Different story, different skyline.

True. Noah sent out a raven, and "It kept flying back and forth until the waters had dried up from the earth." (Genesis 8:7) That bird kept at it with no days off. I think that raven earned a long nap.

This one's true, friend. Genesis 8:7 says Noah "sent out a raven. It kept flying back and forth until the waters had dried up from the earth." The text has the raven going back and forth right up until the waters had dried up. So the card is telling the truth.

Right on. "…the dove found no place to rest her foot, and she returned to him in the ark…" (Genesis 8:9) The waters were still covering the surface of all the earth, so she had nowhere to land. Noah reached out his hand and brought her back inside the ark. I bet she was glad to see that hand.

No nest on this trip. Genesis 8:9 says she found no place to rest her foot and returned to Noah. The waters were still covering the surface of all the earth. So she came back to the ark instead of settling anywhere.

An olive leaf, and a freshly plucked one. "…the dove returned to him in the evening with a freshly plucked olive leaf in her beak." (Genesis 8:11) On her first trip she found no place to rest her foot (Genesis 8:9). This time she's carrying something, and I bet Noah noticed right away.

Fig leaves are in the Bible, but earlier, when Adam and Eve sewed fig leaves together to make coverings for themselves (Genesis 3:7). Here the dove brings back an olive leaf (Genesis 8:11). Fig and olive are two different trees, friend.
Palm branches come much later, when the crowd took palm branches and went out to meet Jesus (John 12:13). The dove isn't carrying one. In Genesis 8:11, it's a freshly plucked olive leaf.

Receded is the word. The text says, "So Noah knew that the waters had receded from the earth." (Genesis 8:11) That comes right after the dove shows up with the freshly plucked olive leaf. Noah didn't need a weather report, just a dove with good timing.

Stilled isn't the word the text uses. Genesis 8:11 says Noah knew the waters had receded from the earth. Receded means pulled back, like a tide leaving the shore. Stilled sounds peaceful, but this verse is about the water going down, not sitting calm.
Not this time. Genesis 8:12 says Noah "waited seven more days and sent out the dove again, but this time she did not return to him." The first two trips, she came back. The third, she didn't.
You've got it. Genesis 8:12 says Noah "sent out the dove again, but this time she did not return to him." Twice she came back to Noah. The third time, she stayed out there.
Dry! "…Noah removed the covering from the ark and saw that the surface of the ground was dry." (Genesis 8:13) After all that water, I bet that was a sight. He's finally looking at ground.
Not anymore. The text says Noah removed the covering and saw that the surface of the ground was dry (Genesis 8:13). The waters had dried up from the earth. The flooding was over.

Leave is the word. God says, "Come out of the ark, you and your wife, along with your sons and their wives." (Genesis 8:16) The earth is fully dry by then (Genesis 8:14). After all that time inside, I bet that was good to hear.

Yes! God says the creatures should come out "…so that they can spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon it." (Genesis 8:17) That means the birds, the livestock and everything that crawls. The animals have a whole earth waiting for them. That's a lot of creatures with a lot of room.

Taking the ark apart never comes up in the text. God's reason is that they can "…spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon it." (Genesis 8:17) The creatures are headed out to fill the earth, not to watch a teardown. Different job, friend.

The clean ones. "…taking from every kind of clean animal and clean bird, he offered burnt offerings on the altar." (Genesis 8:20) Noah builds the altar to the LORD first. Then he makes the offering from the clean animals and birds. Clean is the word that counts here.
True. The LORD says in His heart, "Never again will I curse the ground because of man…" (Genesis 8:21) That's the statement just as the card gives it. A promise like that is worth holding onto.

This one is true, friend. The text has the LORD saying in His heart, "Never again will I curse the ground because of man…" (Genesis 8:21) The card repeats it just as it stands. Sometimes a card is simply telling you the truth, and it's allowed to.

That's what He says. The LORD says, "…even though every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth." (Genesis 8:21) It's a heavy line, and I think it's worth slowing down on. He says it right alongside "Never again will I curse the ground because of man…"

The text says the opposite, and it's a heavy line. The LORD says, "…even though every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth." (Genesis 8:21) Right after that He says, "And never again will I destroy all living creatures as I have done."

Right. What the LORD says in His heart is, "And never again will I destroy all living creatures as I have done." (Genesis 8:21) He promises the opposite of what the card says. So the card has it backwards.

True. God says, "But you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it." (Genesis 9:4) Right before that, He says, "Everything that lives and moves will be food for you…" (Genesis 9:3). So it's a big yes with one rule attached. The catch is the lifeblood.
Yes. God says, "for in His own image God has made mankind." (Genesis 9:6) That's the reason given for treating human life so seriously. The reason is who made people and whose image they carry.

Not quite. God says His covenant is also "…with every living creature that was with you…" (Genesis 9:10). The text names the birds, the livestock and every beast of the earth, every living thing that came out of the ark. The animals are in this covenant right alongside Noah's family.

Right. God says, "Never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood…" (Genesis 9:11) That's the promise of the covenant. He adds, "never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth." Waters were the whole story here, so waters are the promise.

His rainbow! God says, "I have set My rainbow in the clouds, and it will be a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth." (Genesis 9:13) He puts the sign in the clouds, where everybody can see it. Next time you see one, you know whose it is.

Yes. God says, "I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of every kind." (Genesis 9:15) That's what the rainbow is for. In the next verse He says, "…I will see it and remember…" (Genesis 9:16).

Gathering isn't in this verse. When the rainbow appears, God says, "I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of every kind." (Genesis 9:15) Gathering sounds like a roundup, but this is about a promise, not a roundup. The rainbow is the sign in the sky.

Not here. Genesis 9:15 has God saying, "I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of every kind." That's what He does when the rainbow appears. Harvest does get a mention earlier, when seedtime and harvest are said to never cease (Genesis 8:22). But that's a different promise from this one.

Everlasting. God says, "…I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of every kind that is on the earth." (Genesis 9:16) Earlier He called it "a covenant for all generations to come" (Genesis 9:12). That word doesn't have an expiration date.
